========================================================================
Page: https://petercorke.github.io/pgraph-python/export.html
========================================================================

Exporting a graph
*****************

Graphs can be exported to a number of different formats, including dot
(used by GraphViz), Mermaid (a JavaScript-based graph visualization
tool that can be used in Markdown documents), GraphML (an XML-based
format for representing graphs), ELK (a graph layout engine), as well
as various image formats (e.g., PNG, SVG, PDF).

See Visualization for rendering the graph using Matplotlib itself
rather than exporting it.

+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| "export"   | Convert and save the graph in a graph export or image format                               |
+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| "dotfile"  | Export graph as a GraphViz dot file                                                        |
+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Details
=======

Graph.export(filename=None, format=None, **options)

   Convert and save the graph in a graph export or image format

   Parameters:
      * **filename** (*str**, **path-like** or **file object**,
        **optional*) -- destination path or open file, defaults to
        None

      * **format** (*str**, **optional*) -- ""dot"", ""mermaid"",
        ""graphml"", ""elk"" or an image format ""svg"", ""pdf"",
        ""png"" ..., inferred from the extension of "filename" if not
        given

      * **options** ("Any") -- format specific options, see below

   Raises:
      * **ValueError** -- the format is unknown or cannot be inferred,
        or an image format is requested without a "filename"

      * **TypeError** -- an option is not valid for the format

      * **RuntimeError** -- an image format is requested and GraphViz
        is not installed, or fails

   Returns:
      the text if "filename" is None, otherwise None

   Return type:
      str or None

   +---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
   | "format"                  | extensions                | positions                 | options                   |
   |===========================|===========================|===========================|===========================|
   | ""dot""                   | ".dot" ".gv"              | "pos="x,y!""              | "direction",              |
   |                           |                           |                           | "color_components",       |
   |                           |                           |                           | "costs"                   |
   +---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
   | ""mermaid""               | ".mmd" ".mermaid"         | no                        | "direction",              |
   |                           |                           |                           | "color_components",       |
   |                           |                           |                           | "costs", "fence"          |
   +---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
   | ""graphml""               | ".graphml"                | "x", "y", "coord"         | none                      |
   +---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
   | ""elk""                   | ".elk.json" ".elk"        | "x", "y"                  | "size", "layout_options"  |
   +---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+
   | ""svg"" ""pdf"" ""png""   | the same                  | yes, via "neato"          | "engine", "direction",    |
   | ...                       |                           |                           | "color_components",       |
   |                           |                           |                           | "costs"                   |
   +---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------+

   The text formats need nothing beyond the standard library.  The
   image formats run the GraphViz "dot" or "neato" executable.

      >>> from pgraph import UGraph
      >>> g = UGraph()
      >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
      >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,1], name='v2')
      >>> g.add_edge(v1, v2, cost=2)
      Edge{[v1] -- [v2], cost=2}
      >>> print(g.export(format="mermaid", direction="LR"))
      flowchart LR
          n0["v1"]
          n1["v2"]
          n0 ---|"2"| n1

   Note:

     * Output is reproducible: vertices are written in creation order
       and edges in the order of their vertices, not in set order.

     * A file object passed as "filename" is written but not closed. A
       path is opened, and closed even if writing fails.

     * Names are escaped for each format, and Mermaid, GraphML and ELK
       use generated ids so any vertex name is valid.

   -[ For graphs with parallel edges or loops ]-

   Every edge is written, each with its own cost, so parallel edges
   give repeated lines (DOT, Mermaid) or distinct "id" elements
   (GraphML, ELK).  A self-loop is written once, as an edge from a
   vertex to itself.

   Seealso:
      "dotfile()" "showgraph()" "pgraph.exporters"

Graph.dotfile(filename=None, direction=None)

   Export graph as a GraphViz dot file

   Parameters:
      * **filename** (*str**, **path-like** or **file object**,
        **optional*) -- filename to save graph to, defaults to None

      * **direction** (*str**, **optional*) -- layout direction, eg.
        ""LR"", defaults to None

   Return type:
      "None"

   "g.dotfile()" creates the specified file which contains the
   GraphViz code to represent the embedded graph.  By default output
   is to the console.

   This is "export()" with "format="dot"" and edge costs left
   unlabelled, as it has always been.  Use "export()" for other
   formats or for edge labels.

   Note:

     * The graph is undirected if it is a "UGraph"

     * The graph is directed if it is a "DGraph"

   Note:

     The "graphviz" formatters "dot" and "neato" can be used to render
     the graph in various formats including PDF, PNG, JPG, GIF, SVG,
     etc.  The formatters are similar, but "dot" is better suited for
     directed graphs while "neato" is better suited for undirected
     graphs.

      >>> from pgraph import UGraph
      >>> g = UGraph()
      >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
      >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,1], name='v2')
      >>> g.add_edge(v1, v2)
      Edge{[v1] -- [v2], cost=1.414}
      >>> g.dotfile()
      graph {
        "v1" [pos="0,0!"]
        "v2" [pos="1,1!"]
        "v1" -- "v2"
      }

   Note:

     Edge costs are not included in the output.  Use "export()" with
     "costs=True" to include them.

   Note:

     If "filename" is a file object then the file will *not* be closed
     after the GraphViz model is written. Safe for use with
     "sys.stdout" or "sys.stderr".

   Seealso:
      "export()" "showgraph()"

The exporters
=============

"export()" hands the work to the functions of "pgraph.exporters".  The
options of each format are the keyword arguments of its function,
which are passed through "export(..., **options)".  The module also
provides the means to add a format of your own.

Export a graph as text (GraphViz DOT, Mermaid, GraphML, ELK JSON) or
as a rendered image (via the GraphViz command line tools).

This module is reached through "export()", which dispatches on the
format name or the file extension.  Each text exporter is a plain
function "f(graph, **options) -> str", registered with
"register_exporter()", so a user can add a format without touching the
package:

   from pgraph.exporters import register_exporter

   @register_exporter("gexf", ".gexf")
   def gexf(graph, *, version="1.3") -> str:
       ...

None of the text formats needs a dependency beyond the standard
library.  Only the rendered formats ("RENDER_FORMATS") need the
GraphViz executables.

ENGINES = ('dot', 'neato', 'fdp', 'sfdp', 'twopi', 'circo', 'osage', 'patchwork')

   GraphViz layout programs that may be run to render an image

RENDER_FORMATS: dict[str, bool] = {'gif': False, 'jpeg': False, 'jpg': False, 'pdf': False, 'png': False, 'ps': True, 'svg': True}

   image formats produced by running the GraphViz "dot"/"neato"
   executable, mapped to whether the result is text ("True") or binary
   ("False")

register_exporter(name, *extensions)

   Register a text exporter (decorator)

   Parameters:
      * **name** ("str") -- format name used as "export(format=name)"

      * **extensions** ("str") -- file extensions, with the leading
        dot, that select this format when "format" is not given

   Return type:
      "Callable"[["Callable"["...", "str"]], "Callable"["...", "str"]]

   Returns:
      the decorator

   The decorated function is called as "f(graph, **options)" and
   returns the text.  Declare its options as keyword-only parameters
   so that an unknown option is a "TypeError".

get_exporter(name)

   Look up a text exporter by format name

   Parameters:
      **name** ("str") -- format name, eg. ""dot""

   Return type:
      "Callable"["...", "str"]

   Returns:
      the function "f(graph, **options) -> str"

   Raises:
      **ValueError** -- no text exporter has that name; the message
      lists those that do

formats()

   Names of all supported export formats

   Returns:
      text formats followed by rendered image formats

   Return type:
      list of str

format_from_filename(filename)

   Infer an export format from a file name's extension

   Parameters:
      **filename** ("str" | "PathLike" | "IO" | "None") -- path, or a
      file object with a "name" attribute

   Returns:
      the format name, or None if it cannot be decided

   Return type:
      str or None

   Compound extensions such as ".elk.json" are tried before the plain
   suffix.

dot(graph, *, direction=None, color_components=False, costs=True)

   GraphViz DOT text

   Parameters:
      * **direction** ("str" | "None") -- layout direction, "rankdir"
        in DOT, eg. ""LR""

      * **color_components** ("bool") -- fill vertices by connected
        component

      * **costs** ("bool") -- label edges with their cost

   Return type:
      "str"

mermaid(graph, *, direction='TB', color_components=False, costs=True, fence=False)

   Mermaid flowchart text

   Parameters:
      * **direction** ("str") -- ""TB"", ""BT"", ""LR"" or ""RL""

      * **color_components** ("bool") -- fill vertices by connected
        component

      * **costs** ("bool") -- label edges with their cost

      * **fence** ("bool") -- wrap in a Markdown code fence, three
        backticks followed by "mermaid"

   Return type:
      "str"

   Mermaid flowcharts are laid out automatically and cannot pin node
   positions, so vertex coordinates are not represented.  Vertices are
   given generated ids ("n0", "n1", ...) with the real name as the
   label, since names are arbitrary strings but Mermaid ids are not.

graphml(graph)

   GraphML XML text

   Name, component, coordinate ("x", "y" and the full "coord" string
   for higher dimensions) and edge cost are written as "<data>"
   elements with "<key>" declarations.  "edgedefault" follows the
   graph kind.  GraphML has no standard node position outside the
   proprietary yFiles extension, which is not used.

   Return type:
      "str"

elk(graph, *, size=(60, 40), layout_options=None)

   Eclipse Layout Kernel (ELK) JSON graph text

   Parameters:
      * **size** ("tuple"["float", "float"]) -- width and height given
        to every node, which ELK requires

      * **layout_options** ("dict"["str", "str"] | "None") -- ELK
        layout options, merged over the defaults

   Return type:
      "str"

   Unlike GraphML, ELK has native "x" and "y" node fields.  If any
   vertex has a coordinate the "fixed" algorithm is selected so that a
   consumer keeps the positions; otherwise "layered" computes a
   layout.

render(graph, fmt, *, engine=None, direction=None, color_components=False, costs=True)

   Render the graph to an image with the GraphViz executables

   Parameters:
      * **fmt** ("str") -- one of "RENDER_FORMATS"

      * **engine** ("str" | "None") -- GraphViz layout program, one of
        "ENGINES".  Defaults to "neato" if any vertex has a
        coordinate, since it honours pinned positions, else "dot"

   Returns:
      the image

   Return type:
      bytes

   Raises:
      * **ValueError** -- "fmt" or "engine" is not a known name

      * **RuntimeError** -- the layout program is not installed, or
        failed

   Both names are checked against fixed lists and the program is run
   with an argument list and no shell, so neither can carry a command.

========================================================================
Page: https://petercorke.github.io/pgraph-python/planning.html
========================================================================

Path planning
*************

These methods find a path from a start vertex to a goal vertex.
"path_BFS()" finds the path with the fewest edges, while "path_UCS()"
and "path_Astar()" find the path with the lowest total cost.

+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| "path_BFS" | Breadth-first search for path                                                              |
+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| "path_UCS" | Uniform cost search for path                                                               |
+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| "path_Asta | A* search for path                                                                         |
| r"         |                                                                                            |
+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Details
=======

Graph.path_BFS(S, G, verbose=False, summary=False)

   Breadth-first search for path

   Parameters:
      * **S** (*Vertex subclass*) -- start vertex

      * **G** (*Vertex subclass*) -- goal vertex

      * **verbose** ("bool") -- print search progress, defaults to
        False

      * **summary** ("bool") -- print a one-line search summary,
        defaults to False

   Raises:
      * **TypeError** -- "S" or "G" is neither a vertex nor a string

      * **KeyError** -- "S" or "G" is a name not in the graph

      * **ValueError** -- an edge on the path has no cost

   Returns:
      list of vertices from S to G inclusive and path length, or None
      if there is no path

   Return type:
      (list of Vertex subclass, float) or None

   Compute a path from vertex "S" to vertex "G" using breadth-first
   search.  The path is guaranteed to be the shortest in terms of
   number of edges, but not necessarily the cheapest in terms of edge
   costs.  This search is not suited to graphs with edge weights, and
   is inefficient in that it explores all vertices.

   Returns a list of vertices that starts with vertex "S" and ends
   with vertex "G" if possible, otherwise returns None -- so check the
   result before unpacking it.

      >>> from pgraph import UGraph
      >>> g = UGraph()
      >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
      >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,0], name='v2')
      >>> v3 = g.add_vertex(coord=[2,0], name='v3')
      >>> g.add_edge(v1, v2)
      Edge{[v1] -- [v2], cost=1}
      >>> g.add_edge(v2, v3)
      Edge{[v2] -- [v3], cost=1}
      >>> path, length = g.path_BFS(v1, v3)
      >>> print(path)
      [Vertex[v1, coord=(0, 0)], Vertex[v2, coord=(1, 0)], Vertex[v3, coord=(2, 0)]]
      >>> print(length)
      2.0

   Note:

     Self-loops are ignored. If there are parallel edges the cheapest
     is used for the path length.

   Seealso:
      "path_UCS()" "path_Astar()"

Graph.path_UCS(S, G, verbose=False, summary=False)

   Uniform cost search for path

   Parameters:
      * **S** (*Vertex subclass*) -- start vertex

      * **G** (*Vertex subclass*) -- goal vertex

      * **verbose** ("bool") -- print search progress, defaults to
        False

      * **summary** ("bool") -- print a one-line search summary,
        defaults to False

   Raises:
      * **TypeError** -- "S" or "G" is neither a vertex nor a string

      * **KeyError** -- "S" or "G" is a name not in the graph

      * **ValueError** -- an edge examined during the search has no
        cost

   Returns:
      list of vertices from S to G inclusive, path length and search
      tree, or None if there is no path

   Return type:
      (list of Vertex subclass, float, dict) or None

   Compute the lowest-cost path from vertex "S" to vertex "G" using
   uniform cost search.  The path is guaranteed to be the shortest in
   terms of traversed edge cost, but is inefficient in that it
   explores all vertices.

   Returns a list of vertices that starts with vertex "S" and ends
   with vertex "G" if possible, otherwise returns None -- so check the
   result before unpacking it.

   The search tree is returned as dict that maps a vertex to its
   parent.

   The heuristic is the distance metric of the graph, which defaults
   to Euclidean distance.

      >>> from pgraph import UGraph
      >>> g = UGraph()
      >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
      >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,0], name='v2')
      >>> v3 = g.add_vertex(coord=[2,0], name='v3')
      >>> g.add_edge(v1, v2)
      Edge{[v1] -- [v2], cost=1}
      >>> g.add_edge(v2, v3)
      Edge{[v2] -- [v3], cost=1}
      >>> path, length, tree = g.path_UCS(v1, v3)
      >>> print(path)
      [Vertex[v1, coord=(0, 0)], Vertex[v2, coord=(1, 0)], Vertex[v3, coord=(2, 0)]]
      >>> print(length)
      2.0

   Note:

     Self-loops are ignored. If there are parallel edges the cheapest
     is used for the path length.

   Seealso:
      "path_BFS()" "path_Astar()"

Graph.path_Astar(S, G, verbose=False, summary=False)

   A* search for path

   Parameters:
      * **S** (*Vertex subclass*) -- start vertex

      * **G** (*Vertex subclass*) -- goal vertex

      * **verbose** ("bool") -- print search progress, defaults to
        False

      * **summary** ("bool") -- print a one-line search summary,
        defaults to False

   Raises:
      * **TypeError** -- "S" or "G" is neither a vertex nor a string

      * **KeyError** -- "S" or "G" is a name not in the graph

      * **ValueError** -- an edge examined during the search has no
        cost

   Returns:
      list of vertices from S to G inclusive, path length and search
      tree, or None if there is no path

   Return type:
      (list of Vertex subclass, float, dict) or None

   Compute the lowest-cost path from vertex "S" to vertex "G" using
   A*t search.  The path is guaranteed to be the shortest in terms of
   traversed edge cost, and the search is efficient in terms of the
   number of vertices explored.

   Returns a list of vertices that starts with vertex "S" and ends
   with vertex "G" if possible, otherwise returns None -- so check the
   result before unpacking it.

   The search tree is returned as dict that maps a vertex to its
   parent.

   The heuristic is the distance metric of the graph, which defaults
   to Euclidean distance.

      >>> from pgraph import UGraph
      >>> g = UGraph()
      >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
      >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,0], name='v2')
      >>> v3 = g.add_vertex(coord=[2,0], name='v3')
      >>> g.add_edge(v1, v2)
      Edge{[v1] -- [v2], cost=1}
      >>> g.add_edge(v2, v3)
      Edge{[v2] -- [v3], cost=1}
      >>> path, length, tree = g.path_Astar(v1, v3)
      >>> print(path)
      [Vertex[v1, coord=(0, 0)], Vertex[v2, coord=(1, 0)], Vertex[v3, coord=(2, 0)]]
      >>> print(length)
      2.0

   Note:

     Self-loops are ignored. If there are parallel edges the cheapest
     is used for the path length.

   Seealso:
      "heuristic()" "path_BFS()" "path_UCS()"

========================================================================
Page: https://petercorke.github.io/pgraph-python/edges_vertices.html
========================================================================

Edges & Vertices
****************

Underlying data structures
==========================

[image]

The graph class maintains a list of vertices and a dict of edges. For
the undirected case, each vertex maintains a list of edges that
connect to it, and each edge maintains a reference to the two vertices
it connects. In the case of a loop, the edge appears twice in the
vertex's edge list. For the directed case, each vertex maintains two
edge lists: a list of outgoing edges and a list of incoming edges.

The graph class provides methods for adding and removing vertices and
edges (see Adding and removing vertices and edges) and for querying
its structure (see Graph analysis).

What a vertex holds
-------------------

Each vertex has **two** private edge lists, plus a back-pointer to its
graph.

+-----------------+---------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Attribute       | For undirected graphs                                   | For directed graphs            |
|=================|=========================================================|================================|
| "_edgelist"     | the edges *incident on* it                              | the edges *leaving* it         |
+-----------------+---------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| "_inlist"       | empty                                                   | the edges *entering* it        |
+-----------------+---------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| "_graph"        | the graph it belongs to ("None" if standalone)          | the graph it belongs to        |
|                 |                                                         | ("None" if standalone)         |
+-----------------+---------------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------+

Every list entry is a reference to the same "Edge" class object, and
there is exactly one edge object for each edge in the graph.

* **Undirected:** one list does everything, since an undirected edge
  is both "out" and "in".  That is also why a loop is stored twice,
  once for each end, and why it counts 2 towards "degree".

* **Directed:** the two lists are the out-list and the in-list.  A
  loop sits once in each, so "degree" (in + out) is 2 there too.

An example, as lists
--------------------

For these simple graphs

   [image: the example graph drawn as an undirected and as a directed
   graph: two parallel edges e1 and e2 from a to b, e3 from b to c and
   a loop e4 on c][image]

The vertices "a", "b" and "c" and edges "e1" and "e2" are added in
that order. The resulting vertex lists are

+------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Vertex     | "UGraph" "_edgelist"           | "DGraph" "_edgelist"           | "DGraph" "_inlist"             |
| name       |                                |                                |                                |
|============|================================|================================|================================|
| "a"        | "[e1, e2]"                     | "[e1, e2]"                     | "[]"                           |
+------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| "b"        | "[e1, e2, e3]"                 | "[e3]"                         | "[e1, e2]"                     |
+------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| "c"        | "[e3, e4, e4]"                 | "[e4]"                         | "[e3, e4]"                     |
+------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+--------------------------------+

The graph also keeps **every edge once** in "graph._edges" (an
insertion-ordered dict, so "[e1, e2, e3, e4]").

The public view of those lists
------------------------------

+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| Method                         | Returns for "UGraph"                | Returns for "DGraph"                |
|================================|=====================================|=====================================|
| "edges()", "out_edges()"       | a copy of "_edgelist"               | a copy of "_edgelist"               |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| "in_edges()"                   | a copy of "_edgelist"               | a copy of "_inlist"                 |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| "degree"                       | "len(_edgelist)"                    | "len(_edgelist) + len(_inlist)"     |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| "in_degree"                    | "len(_edgelist)"                    | "len(_inlist)"                      |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| "out_degree"                   | "len(_edgelist)"                    | "len(_edgelist)"                    |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| "adjacent()"                   | the far end of each edge in         | the far end of each edge in         |
|                                | "_edgelist"                         | "_edgelist"                         |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
| "incidences()"                 | "adjacent()" paired with            | "adjacent()" paired with            |
|                                | "out_edges()"                       | "out_edges()"                       |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+

All are returned in the order the edges were connected.

Working with vertices and edges directly
========================================

In the earlier examples we did not explicitly create vertices or
edges, but we can do so if we want to. The graph classes provide
methods to create vertices and edges, and to add them to the graph.

   >>> from pgraph import UGraph, Vertex, Edge
   >>> import numpy as np
   >>> g = UGraph()

Next, we will explicitly create two vertices

   >>> v1 = Vertex(np.random.rand(2))
   >>> v2 = Vertex(np.random.rand(2))

and then add them to the graph

   >>> g.add_vertex(v1)
   Vertex[#0, coord=(0.5416, 0.5674)]
   >>> g.add_vertex(v2)
   Vertex[#1, coord=(0.9622, 0.546)]

Our graph now has two vertices, but no edges

   >>> print(g)
   UGraph: 2 vertices, 0 edges, 2 components

We can explicitly create an edge between the two vertices

   >>> e = Edge(v1, v2)

and then add it to the graph

   >>> g.add_edge(e)
   Edge{[#0] -- [#1], cost=0.4212}
   >>> print(g)
   UGraph: 2 vertices, 1 edge, 1 component

Creating the edge and then adding it to the graph, as above, is
equivalent to

   >>> e = Edge()
   >>> e.connect(v1, v2)

Alternatively, we can create a vertex and *connect* it to an existing
vertex, which will implicitly create an edge between the two vertices
and add it to the graph.

   >>> v3 = Vertex(np.random.rand(2))
   >>> g.add_vertex(v3)
   Vertex[#2, coord=(0.1311, 0.5992)]
   >>> v2.connect(v3)
   Edge{[#1] -- [#2], cost=0.8328}
   >>> print(g)
   UGraph: 3 vertices, 2 edges, 1 component

The "connect" method of the vertex class creates an edge between the
two vertices and adds it to the graph. The two vertices must have been
added to the same graph for the edge to be created. The "connect"
method is the same for directed and undirected graphs: the graph
decides how the edge is recorded at its vertices.

Note:

  Wherever a vertex or edge is required, a subclass of the appropriate
  base class can be used. For example, we can create a subclass of
  "Vertex" called "MyVertex" and a subclass of "Edge" called "MyEdge"
  and then create a new graph using these classes, by passing them as
  the "vertex_class" and "edge_class" arguments of the graph
  constructor.

The Vertex class
================

class Vertex(coord=None, name=None)

   Bases: "object"

   A vertex of a graph, directed or undirected.

   A vertex has no direction of its own: how an edge is recorded at
   its ends is decided by the graph it belongs to (see "UGraph" and
   "DGraph").  So there is one vertex class, which can be subclassed
   to give user objects graph capability and passed to the graph as
   "vertex_class".

   Changed in version 1.0: This replaces "UVertex" and "DVertex",
   which are deprecated names for it.  They differed only in how an
   edge was recorded, which is now the graph's decision.

   Each vertex has:
      * "name" which is its key in the graph, so renaming a vertex
        that is in a graph updates the graph

      * "label" an int indicating which graph component contains it,
        read-only: the graph assigns it

      * "coord" the coordinate in an embedded graph (optional)

   and its edges are available from "edges()", "out_edges()" and
   "in_edges()".

   Seealso:
      "Graph" "Edge"

   __init__(coord=None, name=None)

      Create a vertex object

      Parameters:
         * **coord** (*array-like**, **optional*) -- coordinate of the
           vertex for an embedded graph, defaults to None

         * **name** (*str**, **optional*) -- vertex name, defaults to
           None

      Creates a vertex but does not add it to a graph -- use
      "Graph.add_vertex()" for that.

         >>> from pgraph import Vertex
         >>> v1 = Vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
         >>> print(v1)
         [v1]

      Seealso:
         "Graph.add_vertex()"

The Edge class
==============

class Edge(v1=None, v2=None, cost=None, data=None)

   Bases: "object"

   Edge class

   Is used to represent directed and undirected edges.

   Each edge has a cost, arbitrary data, and two vertices "v1" and
   "v2", which are read-only: the start and end vertex for a directed
   edge.

   cost: float | None

      cost of traversing this edge, required for planning methods

   data: Any

      reference to arbitrary data associated with the edge

   Note:

     * An undirected graph is created by having a single edge object
       in the edgelist of _each_ vertex.

     * This class can be inherited to provide user objects with graph
       capability.

     * Inheritance is an alternative to providing arbitrary user data.

     * Pass the subclass as "edge_class" when constructing the graph
       and the graph will create instances of it itself, see "Graph".

   An Edge points to a pair of vertices.  At "connect" time the
   vertices get references back to the Edge object.

   "graph.add_edge(v1, v2)" calls "v1.connect(v2)"

   Seealso:
      "Vertex"

   __init__(v1=None, v2=None, cost=None, data=None)

      Create an edge object

      Parameters:
         * **v1** ("Vertex", optional) -- start of the edge, defaults
           to None

         * **v2** ("Vertex", optional) -- end of the edge, defaults to
           None

         * **cost** (*any**, **optional*) -- edge cost, defaults to
           None

         * **data** (*any**, **optional*) -- edge data, defaults to
           None

      Creates an edge but does not connect it to the vertices or add
      it to the graph.

      If vertices are given, and have associated coordinates, the edge
      cost will be computed according to the distance measure
      associated with the graph.

      "data" is a way of associating any object with the edge, its
      value can be found as the ".data" attribute of the edge.  An
      alternative approach is to subclass the "Edge" class.

      Note:

        To compute edge cost from the vertices, both vertices must
        have already been added to the same graph -- otherwise "cost"
        is left as None rather than raising, since this constructor is
        also used standalone, independent of any graph.

      Seealso:
         "Edge.connect()" "Vertex.connect()"

   connect(v1, v2)

      Attach this edge to a pair of vertices

      Parameters:
         * **v1** (*Vertex subclass*) -- start of the edge

         * **v2** (*Vertex subclass*) -- end of the edge

      Raises:
         * **ValueError** -- either vertex has not been added to a
           graph, or the vertices belong to different graphs

         * **TypeError** -- this edge is not an instance of the
           graph's "Graph.edge_class"

      Return type:
         "None"

      The edge connects vertices "v1" and "v2", and is added to the
      graph that those vertices belong to.

      Warning:

        Intended for an edge that is not yet part of a graph. The
        edge's "v1" and "v2" are overwritten without checking, so
        connecting an edge that is already in a graph leaves it
        referenced from its old vertices as well.

         >>> from pgraph import Vertex, Edge, UGraph
         >>> g = UGraph()
         >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
         >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,1], name='v2')
         >>> e = Edge(cost=1.414)
         >>> e.connect(v1, v2)
         >>> print(e)
         Edge{[v1] -- [v2], cost=1.414}

      Note:

        The vertices must already be added to the graph.

      Seealso:
         "Vertex.connect()"

   property endpoints: list[Vertex]

      The two vertices of this edge

      Returns:
         start and end vertex

      Return type:
         list of Vertex subclass

         >>> from pgraph import Vertex, Edge
         >>> v1 = Vertex(coord=[1,2], name="A")
         >>> v2 = Vertex(coord=[3,4], name="B")
         >>> e = Edge(v1, v2, cost=5.0, data="A to B")
         >>> print(e)
         Edge{[A] -- [B], cost=5} data=A to B
         >>> print(e.endpoints)
         [Vertex[A, coord=(1, 2)], Vertex[B, coord=(3, 4)]]

      Seealso:
         "vertices()"

   next(vertex)

      Return other end of an edge

      Parameters:
         **vertex** (*Vertex subclass*) -- one vertex on the edge

      Raises:
         **ValueError** -- "vertex" is not on the edge

      Returns:
         the other vertex on the edge

      Return type:
         Vertex subclass

      "e.next(v1)" is the vertex at the other end of edge "e", ie. the
      vertex that is not "v1".

         >>> from pgraph import Vertex, Edge
         >>> v1 = Vertex(coord=[1,2], name="A")
         >>> v2 = Vertex(coord=[3,4], name="B")
         >>> e = Edge(v1, v2, cost=5.0, data="A to B")
         >>> print(e)
         Edge{[A] -- [B], cost=5} data=A to B
         >>> e.next(v1)
         Vertex[B, coord=(3, 4)]
         >>> e.next(v2)
         Vertex[A, coord=(1, 2)]

   remove()

      Remove this edge from its graph

      Raises:
         **ValueError** -- the edge is not connected to a graph

      "e.remove()" removes "e" from its graph's own edge collection
      and from its connected vertices' edge lists (both, for an
      undirected edge; the source only, for a directed one -- see
      "Graph.remove_edge()"), and clears "e.v1"/"e.v2" to "None". The
      "Edge" object itself is not deleted -- it becomes an orphaned,
      disconnected shell, and calling "remove()" on it again raises
      "ValueError".

      Note:

        This is a thin convenience wrapper around
        "Graph.remove_edge()".

      Return type:
         None

         >>> from pgraph import UGraph
         >>> g = UGraph()
         >>> v1 = g.add_vertex(coord=[0,0], name='v1')
         >>> v2 = g.add_vertex(coord=[1,1], name='v2')
         >>> e = g.add_edge(v1, v2)
         >>> e.remove()
         >>> print(g)
         UGraph: 2 vertices, 0 edges, 2 components

      Seealso:
         "Graph.remove_edge()" "Vertex.remove()"

   property v1: Vertex | None

      First vertex of the edge, the start vertex for a directed edge

      Returns:
         the vertex, or None if the edge is not connected

      Return type:
         Vertex subclass or None

      Changed in version 1.0: Read-only.  It was a plain attribute, so
      assigning to it on an edge that was in a graph left the graph
      inconsistent: the vertices' edge lists no longer agreed with the
      edge, and the edge could not be removed.  Give the vertices to
      the constructor, "Edge(v1, v2)", or to "connect()" or
      "Vertex.connect()".

      Seealso:
         "v2" "connect()"

   property v2: Vertex | None

      Second vertex of the edge, the end vertex for a directed edge

      Returns:
         the vertex, or None if the edge is not connected

      Return type:
         Vertex subclass or None

      Read-only, see "v1".

      Seealso:
         "v1" "connect()"

   vertices()

      Vertices of an edge (deprecated)

      Returns:
         the two vertices of this edge

      Return type:
         list of Vertex subclass

      Deprecated since version use: "endpoints" instead

========================================================================
Page: https://petercorke.github.io/pgraph-python/policy.html
========================================================================

Object lifecycle and graph-membership policy
********************************************

"Vertex" and "Edge" can both be constructed directly, independent of
any graph. This is deliberate -- it is not an oversight and not a
"factory-only" design -- but it means the rules for what those objects
can and can't do *before* they belong to a graph need to be stated
explicitly rather than left implicit.

Standalone construction
=======================

A vertex or edge built directly, e.g. "Vertex(coord=[1, 2], name="A")"
or "Edge(v1, v2, cost=5.0)", is a fully valid object in its own right.
The main supported use of this is lightweight, graph-independent work:
building a couple of vertices and an edge between them to demonstrate
or test, without needing a graph at all.  Without a graph there is no
metric, so the edge's cost is the one given, or "None".

An object in this state has "._graph is None". It cannot be connected
to anything (see below) until it is added to a graph via
"add_vertex()".

Adding a vertex to a graph
==========================

A vertex is the same for undirected and directed graphs: it has no
direction of its own, and the graph it belongs to decides how an edge
is recorded at its ends.  "add_vertex()" accepts coordinate data, from
which a vertex is built, or an existing "Vertex" that does not belong
to a graph.  A graph given a "vertex_class" only accepts instances of
that class; passing any other vertex raises "TypeError" rather than
being silently accepted or converted.  A vertex that already belongs
to a graph raises "ValueError"; remove it from that graph first.

This is the mechanism that makes graph membership meaningful: once
added, a vertex's "._graph" is fixed to that specific graph instance.

Connecting two vertices
=======================

"v1.connect(v2)" (and the equivalent "graph.add_edge(v1, v2)")
requires **both vertices to already belong to the same graph**:

* If either vertex has not been added to any graph ("._graph is
  None"), "connect()" raises "ValueError".

* If the two vertices belong to different graph instances, "connect()"
  raises "ValueError".

There is no such thing as connecting an "undirected" vertex to a
"directed" one, since a vertex is neither: the kind of edge is the
graph's, so the same-graph check above is the only one needed.

Constructing an "Edge" directly
===============================

"Edge(v1, v2)" (without going through "connect()") does not raise if
the vertices aren't graph-connected -- this constructor is also the
supported standalone-use path described above, so it stays permissive.
Instead:

* If an explicit "cost" is given, it is used as-is.

* Otherwise, the edge cost is auto-computed from vertex coordinates
  via the graph's metric *only if* both vertices are added to the same
  graph. Otherwise "cost" is left as "None" rather than raising.

This means a bare "Edge(v1, v2)" with orphaned or cross-graph vertices
is a valid object with "cost=None" -- it is only the *connecting*
operations ("connect()", "add_edge()") that enforce the graph-
membership invariant strictly.

Summary
=======

+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Operation                         | Requires graph membership?        | Failure mode                      |
|===================================|===================================|===================================|
| "Vertex()"                        | No                                | --                                |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| "Edge(v1, v2)"                    | No (cost falls back to "None" if  | --                                |
|                                   | ungraphed/cross-graph)            |                                   |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| "graph.add_vertex(v)"             | "v" must be of the graph's        | "TypeError" on a vertex of        |
|                                   | "vertex_class" and not already in | another class, "ValueError" if it |
|                                   | a graph, or coordinate data       | is already in a graph             |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| "v1.connect(v2)" /                | Both vertices must already belong | "ValueError" if either is         |
| "graph.add_edge(v1, v2)"          | to the same graph                 | ungraphed or they belong to       |
|                                   |                                   | different graphs                  |
+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
